cards.front: Tiny 1-2 mm white keratin-filled cysts on a newborn's nose and cheeks that resolve spontaneously are [___].
cards.context: Milia are superficial keratin retention cysts, very common in neonates. No treatment is needed — they exfoliate within weeks. Distinguish from neonatal acne and oral Epstein pearls.

cards.front: The five CRASH features of Kawasaki disease are conjunctivitis, [___], adenopathy, strawberry tongue and hand and foot changes.
cards.context:
CRASH is the retrieval handle: Conjunctivitis, Rash, Adenopathy, Strawberry tongue, Hands and feet. Fever is required on top of these, not one of them.

The features accumulate rather than appearing together, so a child seen early can look incomplete and still have the disease.

Conjunctivitis is bilateral and non-purulent, and the node qualifies at 1.5 cm or more, usually on one side.

cards.front: Pancreatic insufficiency affects ~85% of CF patients, causing steatorrhoea; treat with PERT (Creon) with every [___].
cards.context:
Pancreatic exocrine ducts plug with thick secretions → progressive acinar fibrosis → reduced enzyme delivery to gut → fat and protein malabsorption.

PERT (Creon) provides exogenous pancreatic enzymes: lipase, protease and amylase. Adjust dose to symptoms.

cards.front: A well 5-year-old has 20 pearly umbilicated papules on the trunk for 4 months; the parents want them removed. The advice is that they resolve without treatment within [___].
cards.context:
Molluscum is a poxvirus infection that clears on its own over 6 to 18 months once immunity develops. Treatment is for cosmetic or social reasons only and risks scarring.

The exception is the immunocompromised child, in whom hundreds of lesions can persist and need a dermatologist.

cards.front: A 6-week-old with a raised immunoreactive trypsinogen and one CFTR variant on newborn screening has a sweat chloride of 45 mmol/L (normal <30). For cystic fibrosis this result is [___].
cards.context:
The diagnostic line is 60 mmol/L, and below 30 makes cystic fibrosis unlikely. A value between the two neither confirms nor excludes it.

The CF team repeats the sweat test and extends CFTR gene analysis, because some infants in this band do have cystic fibrosis.

The trap is reading any value above normal as diagnostic.

cards.front: Immediate replantation of a child’s avulsed permanent incisor is not possible. According to RCH guidance, the preferred readily available storage fluid during urgent transfer is [___].
cards.context:
Keep the tooth moist while arranging urgent dental assessment. Handle the crown and avoid scrubbing the root.

This pathway is for permanent teeth. An avulsed baby tooth is not replanted because treatment must protect the developing permanent tooth.

cards.front: Allergies to milk, [___], soy, and wheat have high rates of resolution in childhood.
cards.context:
Cow's milk, egg, soy, wheat allergies are typically driven by conformational protein epitopes degraded by cooking + digestion — many children tolerate baked egg or extensively heated milk before raw.

Peanut, tree nut, fish, shellfish target heat-stable epitopes — cooking doesn't help and only ~20% outgrow them.

reference.title: Position Paper: Oral Immunotherapy for Food Allergy

cards.front: Homemade ORS: 1 L water + [___] tsp sugar + ½ tsp salt.
cards.context: Prefer commercial low-osmolarity ORS. Homemade fallback: 1 L clean water + 6 tsp sugar + ½ tsp salt — enough glucose for SGLT without a lethal salt load.

cards.front: If lumbar puncture is unsafe or would delay treatment in a septic neonate, start meningitis-covering [___] immediately and perform LP after stabilisation.
cards.context:
Perform LP promptly and ideally before antibiotics when it is indicated and safe. Haemodynamic instability, impaired consciousness, focal signs or coagulopathy may make immediate LP unsafe.

If LP is contraindicated or would materially delay treatment, cover meningitis now and sample CSF after stabilisation; a delayed LP is safer than delayed antimicrobials.

cards.front: A 2-year-old is not yet walking. Within the ADING framework, the domain that asks about prematurity and perinatal insult is antenatal, and establishing whether a second stream is also delayed matters because delay across two or more domains defines [___] developmental delay.
cards.context:
This is ADING used as a diagnostic instrument rather than recited as a checklist. A 2-year-old not yet walking is a developmental red flag, but the framework is what turns that into a differential.

The antenatal domain asks about prematurity and perinatal insult. The nutrition and growth domains ask whether this is part of faltering growth, and the immunisation domain matters for infection-related causes.

Delay in two or more streams is global delay and widens the workup, whereas isolated motor delay narrows it.

cards.front: A 9-year-old's first afebrile seizure, in class, began with jerking of her right hand, then spread to all four limbs. An hour later she is back to normal with no deficit. The paediatrician's imaging plan is [___].
cards.context:
Jerking that starts in one hand is a focal onset, even once it spreads to all four limbs, and a focal onset raises the chance of a structural brain lesion.

With her back to baseline and no deficit, imaging can wait. MRI finds cortical dysplasia, hippocampal sclerosis and some tumours that CT misses, without radiation.

Urgent CT is kept for a child who has not returned to baseline, has a persisting new deficit, or has had head trauma.

cards.front: Physiological neonatal jaundice reflects immaturity of the liver's bilirubin-[___] enzyme (UGT).
cards.context:
The liver conjugates bilirubin using UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT). In the first days of life this enzyme is immature, so bilirubin clears slowly.

That immaturity — not disease — is why mild jaundice appearing on day 2-3 is physiological and fades as the enzyme matures.

cards.front: Continuous oxygen-driven salbutamol nebulisation is reserved for [___] asthma, rather than being the automatic next step after one inadequate puffer-and-spacer response.
cards.context:
An inadequate response to initial puffer-and-spacer treatment requires reassessment of severity, not automatic continuous nebulisation.

For severe asthma, continue high-dose salbutamol by pMDI and spacer when feasible; use intermittent oxygen-driven nebulised salbutamol if the child cannot use a spacer.

Add ipratropium in the first hour, give a systemic corticosteroid early and seek senior review. Continuous oxygen-driven salbutamol nebulisation is reserved for life-threatening asthma, with immediate senior/ICU input.

cards.front: Mild paediatric gastro dehydration: rehydrate with ORS (oral rehydration solution) (formulated for sodium-glucose co-transport); avoid [___] drinks (osmotic load worsens diarrhoea).
cards.context:
ORS (Hydralyte, Gastrolyte) maximises gut water absorption via the sodium-glucose co-transporter — glucose entering the enterocyte drags sodium, and water follows osmotically.

High-sugar fluids (juice, cordial, soft/sports drinks) do the opposite — excess glucose isn't matched by sodium, so the osmotic load pulls water INTO the lumen and worsens diarrhoea.

Plain water has no glucose to drive uptake at all; the fixed Na 60-90 / glucose 75-110 mmol/L ratio is engineered for this. Single-dose ondansetron before ORS reduces vomiting and improves oral rehydration success.

cards.front: Universal newborn hearing screen target ages: screen by [___] month, diagnose by 3 months, intervene by 6 months — closes the critical window for language development.
cards.context:
The 1-3-6 rule for newborn hearing screening: screen by 1 month (OAE first-line, ABR for NICU), confirm any failed screen with audiology by 3 months. Start intervention (hearing aids, early-intervention) by 6 months.

The targets aren't arbitrary — the first 6 months are the critical language-scaffolding window, and delays past it measurably impair lifelong speech outcomes.

In Australia ~98% are screened by 1 month; compliance falls off at diagnosis and intervention, which is where infants slip through.

cards.front: In severe bronchiolitis, IV fluids are given at [___] maintenance to avoid pulmonary oedema from ADH secretion.
cards.context:
Severe respiratory disease causes non-osmotic ADH release (SIADH-like physiology), so a child given full maintenance fluids retains free water and risks pulmonary oedema and dilutional hyponatraemia.

Restricting to 2/3 maintenance with an isotonic solution (0.9% saline + dextrose) buys back the safety margin without dehydrating the child.

cards.front: Hirschsprung disease: absence of ganglion cells in distal bowel; most commonly [___] (short-segment, 80%); diagnose with suction rectal biopsy.
cards.context:
Hirschsprung is congenital absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus of distal bowel — the failure of neural crest cell migration during embryogenesis.

Short-segment (rectosigmoid only) is commonest at 80%; long-segment and total colonic less common but more severe.

Diagnosis: suction rectal biopsy (gold standard) showing absent ganglion cells + hypertrophied nerves.

cards.front: Most common cause of paediatric OSA is [___] hypertrophy; first-line treatment for this pattern is adenotonsillectomy.
cards.context:
Paediatric OSA often reflects adenotonsillar hypertrophy, especially at age 2-8 when lymphoid tissue is largest relative to the airway.

For this pattern, adenotonsillectomy is first-line. It often improves symptoms and the apnoea-hypopnoea index, but residual OSA is more likely with severe disease, obesity, older age or comorbidity.

Untreated OSA can affect behaviour, growth and cardiovascular health. Persistent symptoms warrant reassessment.

cards.front: A previously well, hungry baby who begins forceful non-bilious vomiting at [___] weeks of age, after an initial period of normal feeding, is in the classic pyloric-stenosis window.
cards.context:
Timing separates the surgical vomiters: obstruction that develops after birth appears only after an initial stretch of normal feeding, whereas congenital obstruction declares itself in the first days of life.

A hungry baby who vomits forcefully straight after a feed and then demands another fits the acquired gastric-outlet picture, not gastroenteritis.

cards.front: Tumour lysis syndrome metabolic derangement: high K⁺, high phosphate, high urate, low [___]; prevent with hydration + allopurinol/rasburicase.
cards.context:
Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is rapid cell death dumping intracellular contents into circulation, classically after starting chemo for high-tumour-burden malignancies (ALL, Burkitt's lymphoma).

Causes AKI (urate crystals + calcium phosphate deposition), cardiac arrhythmia.

Prevention: aggressive hydration + allopurinol (or rasburicase for high-risk).

cards.front: A limping primary-school boy with hip pain referred to the knee, no fever and full weight-bearing fits Perthes disease, which typically presents at [___] years of age.
cards.context:
Perthes is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis and belongs to the primary-school boy; SUFE belongs to the overweight adolescent around the growth spurt.

Pain is often referred to the knee and the child is afebrile and still weight-bearing; fever with refusal to bear weight points to septic arthritis at any age.

The younger the onset, the more growth remains for the femoral head to remodel, so young children are usually contained and observed while older children more often need surgery.

cards.front: Cyanotic newborn not improving with oxygen (suspected duct-dependent CHD): start [___] (alprostadil) infusion to maintain ductal patency while awaiting echo.
cards.context:
Duct-dependent CHD relies on a patent ductus arteriosus for either pulmonary flow (pulmonary/tricuspid atresia, severe pulmonary stenosis) or systemic flow (HLHS, critical aortic stenosis, coarctation).

The duct normally closes in the first days of life — exactly when these babies crash. Empirical PGE1 (alprostadil 0.01-0.05 µg/kg/min IV) keeps it open by relaxing ductal smooth muscle.

Give it to any cyanotic or collapsed neonate with duct-dependent CHD on the differential, even before echo. An unnecessary start is low-cost (apnoea, fever, hypotension); NOT starting risks a dead infant.

cards.front: A normal thymus permits visualisation of pulmonary vessels through it and never [___] the airway — unlike a mediastinal mass.
cards.context:
Two features separate a normal thymus from a mediastinal mass, and both are about what it does NOT do.

Pulmonary vessels remain visible through it because it is not very radio-opaque, and it never compresses the airway or adjacent vasculature. A mass does both.

cards.front: In the weeks after birth, red cells carrying the high-oxygen-affinity [___] are cleared faster than the marrow replaces them with adult haemoglobin, which is one driver of the physiological anaemia at 6-8 weeks.
cards.context:
Fetal red cells are built for a low-oxygen placenta: their haemoglobin binds oxygen more avidly than the adult form. Once the lungs take over, that high affinity is no longer needed.

Three things then drop the haemoglobin together: better oxygenation switches off erythropoietin, short-lived fetal cells are cleared, and rapid growth dilutes the red cell mass.

The nadir of about 95-110 g/L at 6-8 weeks is normal and self-resolves; investigate a fall below the age-specific threshold or any other worrying feature. In preterm babies the nadir comes earlier and deeper.

cards.front: Forced immersion burns show a [___] with uniform depth and sparing of flexion creases, distinguishing them from accidental splash burns.
cards.context:
When a child is held in hot water, the skin contacts liquid at a single static level — producing a sharp horizontal line between burned and unburned tissue.

Accidental spills produce splash patterns: irregular borders, asymmetric depth, and no spared creases because the child moves.

cards.front: A 6-year-old finishes a 4-day burst of prednisolone for acute asthma. The course should be stopped [___], without a taper.
cards.context:
The taper decision is about cumulative adrenal-axis exposure, not a universal day-count threshold. A short burst can be stopped without weaning.

Longer or repeated systemic courses need individual review; repeated bursts should also trigger a preventer and adherence review.

cards.front: A well non-Indigenous 6-month-old has already had pneumococcal conjugate at 2 and 4 months. The next routine pneumococcal dose on the NIP is at [___], not today; the extra 6-month dose is for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and specified medical-risk conditions.
cards.context:
The 6-month pneumococcal conjugate dose is the extra primary dose in the 3+1 schedule used for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and for children with specified medical-risk conditions.

A healthy non-Indigenous infant is on 2+1 (2, 4 and 12 months only). Offering that extra 6-month dose to every child is the error of reading an at-risk row as if it were universal.

cards.front: HSP is usually supportive, but significant abdominal pain or GI involvement is treated with [___].
cards.context:
Most HSP is managed supportively, but significant GI involvement (severe colicky abdominal pain, GI bleeding) is the indication to add corticosteroids.

Corticosteroids shorten the abdominal pain and may reduce the intussusception risk. Renal involvement is the main determinant of long-term prognosis.

cards.front: An adolescent with exudative tonsillitis develops a maculopapular rash after amoxicillin. The likely underlying infection is [___]; this rash alone neither proves nor excludes penicillin allergy.
cards.context:
A maculopapular rash after amoxicillin during EBV infection can be transient, but true drug hypersensitivity also occurs. EBV alone cannot settle the allergy question.

Document the drug, timing and reaction features. Record suspected allergy pending assessment and follow the local drug-allergy pathway; testing belongs in a controlled clinical setting.

cards.front: A 5-week-old settled since birth develops escalating projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds, then demands re-feeding straight away. Onset inside the 2-8-week window makes [___] the diagnosis, not worsening reflux.
cards.context:
Age is the hinge separating the two vomiting stories. Reflux is present from the early weeks, effortless, and the baby stays content.

New forceful vomiting that escalates feed by feed in a previously settled infant of this age is outlet obstruction until proven otherwise — examine for the olive and check a venous gas before any feed trial.

cards.front: A 4-month-old with limited hip abduction is imaged first with [___], not a pelvic X-ray.
cards.context: A 4-month-old hip is still mostly cartilage, so the ossific nucleus is not a reliable radiographic landmark yet. Ultrasound shows the cartilaginous head sitting in the acetabulum and is first-line until about 6 months.

cards.front: ADING separates nutrition, which is what the child takes in, from [___], which is the plotted trajectory that results.
cards.context:
Nutrition and growth are deliberately separate letters, because they answer different questions. Nutrition is what goes in — breast or formula, volumes, solids, appetite, food refusal.

 Growth is the plotted result over time.

A growth chart cannot tell you about intake, and a feeding history cannot tell you whether the child is thriving, so a history that collapses the two loses the link between them.

cards.front: Children with HbSS develop functional [___] by age 5 → susceptibility to encapsulated organisms; need penicillin prophylaxis + pneumococcal/meningococcal vaccination.
cards.context:
Repeated splenic infarction from sickling causes functional asplenia by age 5 in HbSS — the spleen is shrunken, fibrotic, and non-functional.

Penicillin prophylaxis from diagnosis (often lifelong), pneumococcal + meningococcal vaccination.

cards.front: Paediatric stool consistency is graded on the shared pictorial [___] stool chart (types 1–7).
cards.context:
Parent and clinician descriptions of stool ('runny', 'soft', 'pellets') are inconsistent. A shared pictorial scale lets you grade consistency for constipation, diarrhoea, and treatment response.

In paediatrics the same seven-type chart used in adults is the usual shared language.

cards.front: The airflow obstruction in asthma is characteristically [___] — it improves after a bronchodilator.
cards.context: Two features define asthma: the obstruction REVERSES with a bronchodilator, and the airways over-react to multiple triggers (exercise, allergens, cold air). Reversibility is what separates it from fixed obstruction.

cards.front: A 2-year-old has weight loss and a firm, irregular mass crossing the midline. Ultrasound shows a suprarenal mass encasing vessels with calcification. The working diagnosis is [___].
cards.context:
The paediatric team is deciding what a suprarenal mass represents after ultrasound. A mass above and displacing the kidney follows the sympathetic chain rather than arising from renal tissue.

Neuroblastoma can occur along the sympathetic chain, but the adrenal medulla is its commonest primary site. Cross-sectional imaging and urine catecholamine metabolites follow this localisation step.

cards.front: CGD: defective neutrophil oxidative burst; recurrent bacterial and [___] infections; granuloma formation; diagnose with DHR test.
cards.context:
Chronic granulomatous disease: defective NADPH oxidase means neutrophils can phagocytose but can't kill catalase-positive organisms (Staph aureus, Burkholderia, Aspergillus, Nocardia, Serratia).

Diagnosis: dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry (DHR test).

Treatment: lifelong prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole + itraconazole; HSCT for cure.

cards.front: Cerebral palsy: non-progressive motor disorder from developing-brain injury; prevalence [___] per 1000 live births; spastic is the most common motor type.
cards.context:
Cerebral palsy is a NON-PROGRESSIVE motor disorder caused by injury to the developing brain — the brain injury itself is fixed but motor manifestations may evolve as the child grows. Prevalence 2 per 1000 live births.

Classified by topography (hemiplegia, diplegia, quadriplegia) and motor type (spastic ~80%, dyskinetic, ataxic).

Risk factors: prematurity, low birthweight, perinatal asphyxia, neonatal encephalopathy.

cards.front: Croup is a clinical diagnosis; alarm features include agitation, drowsiness, persistent stridor at rest. [___] is a late sign — by then the child is in respiratory failure.
cards.context:
Croup is a clinical diagnosis — barking cough plus inspiratory stridor in a 1-2 year old. Imaging doesn't change management; reserve for atypical cases or to rule out foreign body.

Hypoxia is a LATE sign because croup obstruction is mainly inspiratory; by the time SpO2 drops, the child is in significant respiratory failure.

cards.front: Pancreatic insufficiency affects ~85% of CF patients, causing [___]; treat with PERT (Creon) with every meal/snack.
cards.context:
Pancreatic exocrine ducts plug with thick secretions → progressive acinar fibrosis → reduced enzyme delivery to gut → fat and protein malabsorption.

PERT (Creon) provides exogenous pancreatic enzymes: lipase, protease and amylase. Adjust dose to symptoms.

cards.front: Macrogol is not absorbed and simply holds water in the bowel lumen, which places it in the [___] class of laxatives preferred for months-long maintenance of childhood functional constipation.
cards.context:
Macrogol retains water in the bowel lumen, softening stool. It is a first-line maintenance option after disimpaction, but it can still cause cramps or diarrhoea.

Persistent symptoms need review of adherence, stool burden and dose. A stimulant may be added for selected children under a treatment plan; avoid giving it against impacted stool.

Maintenance often continues for months and is reduced gradually after regular painless stools are established. Stopping too early can allow the withholding cycle to recur.

cards.front: Croup is caused by [___] virus; peak age ~2 years; classic triad of barking cough, hoarse voice, stridor.
cards.context:
Parainfluenza causes ~75% of croup; RSV, adenovirus, influenza, and rhinovirus account for the rest.

Symptoms classically worsen overnight from supine position and increased oedema.

cards.front: After nasal trauma the septum must always be inspected, because an undrained septal haematoma devascularises the septal [___] and causes perforation or abscess. Drainage is urgent, not deferred to review.
cards.context:
Epistaxis and nasal trauma are usually benign, which is exactly why the one time-critical finding gets missed. Every child with nasal trauma needs the septum inspected.

 A septal haematoma strips the mucoperichondrium off the cartilage, which depends on it for blood supply, so untreated it necroses within days — giving septal perforation or abscess and a saddle-nose deformity.

It needs urgent drainage, not review in a week; associated fractures are reduced within 7 to 10 days.

cards.front: A two-month-old has tears overflowing onto one cheek and recurrent crusting from early infancy. Examination finds no conjunctival inflammation. The likely cause is congenital [___].
cards.context:
Impaired drainage lets tears collect on the eye and spill onto the cheek. Discharge can accompany blocked drainage.

A painful red swelling near the inner corner, fever or a generally unwell infant suggests infection and needs prompt assessment.

cards.front: Every child admitted with suspected acute rheumatic fever has an [___], even without a murmur, because subclinical valvulitis found on it counts as carditis.
cards.context:
Auscultation misses rheumatic valvulitis that the scan detects, and subclinical valve involvement is a major manifestation in high- and low-risk groups alike.

The scan also sets a baseline for the valves, which shapes how long secondary prophylaxis continues and how often the child is followed.

An ECG is mandatory too, looking for a prolonged PR interval or higher-grade heart block.

cards.front: A 5-week-old is jaundiced with pale chalky stools and dark urine, and her conjugated bilirubin is raised. The cause that must not be missed, because surgery works best before about 60 days of age, is [___].
cards.context:
Pale stools and dark urine mean bile is not reaching the gut. Jaundice beyond 2 weeks, or any pale stool, needs a split bilirubin, not reassurance.

The extrahepatic bile ducts are progressively obliterated, and the operation is the Kasai portoenterostomy. It is about a quarter of neonatal cholestasis in referral centres.

A normal ultrasound does not exclude it, so a suspected case is discussed with a tertiary paediatric service within 24 hours.

cards.front: About [___] new cancers are diagnosed per 100,000 Australian children aged 0–14 each year.
cards.context: AIHW data for 2011–2015 report about 16 new cancers per 100,000 Australian children aged 0–14 each year. Unlike adult epithelial cancers, paediatric cancers are usually leukaemias or embryonal tumours.

cards.front: Type 1 DM is the most common form in children — autoimmune destruction of beta cells; classic presentation: polyuria, polydipsia, [___], fatigue.
cards.context:
Type 1 diabetes mellitus is the dominant form in children — autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, leading to absolute insulin deficiency.

May present in DKA (vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul respirations, drowsiness).

Type 2 diabetes in children is rising with obesity but still less common; classic presentation is asymptomatic incidental finding.

cards.front: First-line treatment for congenital long QT syndrome is a [___].
cards.context:
Congenital long QT syndrome: ion-channel mutations prolong ventricular repolarisation, predisposing to torsades de pointes.

LQT1 (KCNQ1) is exercise-triggered (especially swimming). LQT2 (KCNH2) responds to auditory triggers. LQT3 (SCN5A) occurs during sleep.

First-line treatment: beta-blockers (nadolol/propranolol). ICD if survived cardiac arrest.

cards.front: A school asthma first-aid plan for sudden wheeze starts with 4 puffs of [___] via a spacer (4 breaths per puff), repeated after 4 minutes if needed.
cards.context:
Asthma first aid follows the 4×4×4 rule: 4 puffs through a spacer, 4 breaths per puff, wait 4 minutes — repeat while organising help if there is no improvement.

In a distressed child the spacer matters as much as the drug: it removes the need to coordinate actuation with inhalation, so the dose actually reaches the airways.

cards.front: The most common congenital heart lesion overall is [___]; the most common cyanotic congenital lesion presenting *after* the neonatal period is TOF.
cards.context:
Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most common CHD overall — a left-to-right shunt. Cyanotic lesions are less common but more dramatic.

Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the commonest cyanotic CHD overall. Timing depends on RV outflow obstruction: severe TOF may be cyanotic at birth, while milder “pink” TOF may become cyanotic later.

Transposition of the great arteries (TGA) is commonest in the first week — ductal-dependent for mixing.
